footer.description: Two quick games that turn startup theory into decisions you can feel. Built for university startup weeks, pitch nights and founder mixers.
footer.disclaimer: Educational simulation. Multiples are simplified and not financial advice. Pitch votes are event feedback, not investment offers.

hero.body: A $10,000 portfolio. Five real startups. One room full of student pitches. Play the two games that turn startup theory into decisions you can feel.
hero.social: Built for founders, aspiring investors, and the merely curious. No finance degree required.

games.title: Two ways to play.
games.body: Play in any order. Each game takes less time than a coffee break and ends with something to argue about.
games.investBody: Start with $10,000. Back five real companies before you know how they ended. Then fast-forward five years and live with it.
games.pitchBody: Swipe on real student pitches. Submit your own card. Then see which niches, ask sizes, and ideas the room actually rewards.
games.pitchCardPitch: Reusable takeaway boxes, tracked by app.

why.title: Startup theory is tidy.
why.body: These games are built around the messy part: choosing under uncertainty, then discovering what your choices reveal about you.

lessons.title: Risk only feels real when it is yours
lessons.body: Allocating someone else's money is easy. Watching a $2,500 cheque become zero teaches more than a lecture slide ever will.

lessons.title: The best story does not always win
lessons.body: Juicero had design, capital, and headlines. Airbnb had air mattresses. History rewards evidence, not volume.

lessons.title: A room has a personality
lessons.body: Swipe data exposes what your audience actually rewards: niche, ask size, founder signal, or raw memorability.

board.title: Student pitches, ready for your verdict.
board.submitTitle: Got a startup of your own?
board.submitBody: Build a card in two minutes. No deck, no login.
board.dataTitle: Every vote becomes a data point.
board.dataBody: See niche heat, ask-size bias, and what the room rewards most.

cta.body: The best way to understand risk is to make a decision and see what happens next. We made that loop fit inside a coffee break.
cta.footnote: No sign-up · no real money · all the lessons

intro.body: Some of these companies became legends. Some became cautionary tales. All of them looked uncertain when the cheque was written. Your job: decide who gets your money before history reveals the answer.
intro.buyingBody: A lesson in risk, timing, and the stories we tell ourselves when a pitch sounds too good to fail.
intro.rulesBody: There is no perfect portfolio. The point is to make a call, see the consequences, and notice your own pattern.

steps.title: Read the pitch
steps.body: Five real startups, frozen at the moment they needed money. You see the story and the risk — never the outcome.

steps.title: Write the cheque
steps.body: Deploy any amount from your $10,000. Go big on one bet, spread it around, or pass entirely. No take-backs.

steps.title: Fast-forward five years
steps.body: Watch the portfolio move year by year, then unpack what history did to your decisions and why.

stage.hidden: The outcome stays hidden until the end. Judge the business, not the brand you know today.
stage.committed: {amount} committed to {name} · {cash} would stay in cash

simulation.title: Five years,
simulation.body: The portfolio moves with the historical trajectory of each company. Watch the narrative, then see what it cost you.

results.protected: You protected capital. You also capped the upside. Both are choices.
results.full: Every position mattered. That is what full deployment feels like.

armchair.label: Armchair Capitalist
armchair.blurb: You kept every dollar. Safe, comfortable, and completely unexposed to the upside.

unicorn.label: Unicorn Whisperer
unicorn.blurb: You found the outliers and gave them enough room to compound. That is rarer than it looks.

seedSavant.label: Seed-Stage Savant
seedSavant.blurb: You balanced conviction with enough diversification to catch a winner without needing a perfect call.

steady.label: Steady Hand
steady.blurb: You protected the downside and still put money to work. Not flashy — but the fund survives.

tuition.label: Tuition Paid
tuition.blurb: The portfolio took a hit, but the lesson is worth more than the paper loss. Most LPs never get this cheap a lesson.

hype.label: Hype Survivor
hype.blurb: One good call could not carry the book. Concentration in the wrong places did the damage.

fullSend.label: Full-Send Historian
fullSend.blurb: You went all in on a story. History has a funny way of charging tuition for that.

reality.label: Risk Appetite, Meet Reality
reality.blurb: You spread the bets but found the zeros. Diversification helps — it does not turn bad businesses into good ones.

dryPowder.title: Dry powder has a cost
dryPowder.body: You finished with {amount} untouched. Cash protects you from ruin, but every dollar sitting out also sits out of the upside.

fullDeploy.title: You deployed every dollar
fullDeploy.body: Full deployment signals conviction. It also removes your ability to double down when a company starts winning. Reserves are a strategic asset.

reserve.title: You kept a real reserve
reserve.body: You put money to work without emptying the tank. That optionality is how funds survive their first bad vintage.

concentration.title: Concentration cuts both ways
concentration.body: More than half of your invested capital went into {name}. When it works, that feels like genius. When it does not, one decision owns the whole story.

portfolio.title: You built a portfolio, not a lottery ticket
portfolio.body: You spread capital across {count} companies. That does not guarantee a win, but it keeps any single failure from ending the game.

fewBets.title: Few bets, high variance
fewBets.body: You only backed {count} companies. Fewer positions means every call matters more — in both directions.

greatStory.title: A great story is not a business
greatStory.body: {name} had attention, capital, and a narrative. What it lacked was durable unit economics. {lesson}

signal.title: Signal hides inside weird
signal.body: None of these companies looked normal at the start. You looked past the surface and backed evidence of a real behaviour change.

juicero.tagline: A $400 Wi-Fi juicer for $5 juice packs.
juicero.description: Juicero raised $120M to make cold-press juice as easy as coffee. The press was beautifully engineered — and completely unnecessary. Its juice packs could be squeezed by hand.
juicero.pitch: Cold-press juice at home without the cleanup. A connected press, compostable packs, and a subscription that keeps the fridge full.
juicero.risk: Premium hardware, a recurring subscription on top, and a product customers may not actually need.

outcome.headline: Squeezed out
outcome.summary: A viral video showed the $400 press was no better than human hands. Juicero cut the price, then shut down in 2017.
outcome.lesson: Hype can raise a round. It cannot manufacture a reason to exist.

milestones: Juicero launches its $699 press to design-world applause.
Bloomberg shows the juice packs can be squeezed by hand. Uh-oh.
Price cut to $399. The internet remains unconvinced.
Juicero shuts down and tries to sell its machines.
The $400 press becomes an eBay curiosity.

pets-com.tagline: The sock puppet that raised $82.5M and died in 268 days.
pets-com.description: Pets.com became the poster child of the dot-com boom with a Super Bowl ad and a lovable sock puppet. The less cute part: selling 50-pound bags of dog food below cost.
pets-com.pitch: Everything your pet needs, delivered to the door. We will spend whatever it takes to own the category before anyone else does.
pets-com.risk: Heavy products, thin margins, and a customer acquisition cost that eats the entire basket.

outcome.headline: Dot-com casualty
outcome.summary: Pets.com went public in February 2000 and liquidated nine months later. Its assets sold for roughly $11M after raising $300M in total.
outcome.lesson: A memorable mascot is not a moat. Unit economics still have to work.

milestones: A Super Bowl ad makes the sock puppet a household name.
IPO lands — then the dot-com bubble starts to hiss.
Liquidation. The sock puppet is sold off with the warehouse.
The domain changes hands. The lesson sticks around.
Pets.com is a case study in spending your way to nowhere.

airbnb.tagline: Air mattresses on a living-room floor. Now a travel empire.
airbnb.description: In 2007, two designers could not pay rent. They put three air mattresses in their loft and charged conference-goers to stay. Investors called it weird. Guests called it magic.
airbnb.pitch: Stay in someone's spare room instead of a hotel. We handle trust, payments, and photos. Cheaper for guests, lucrative for hosts.
airbnb.risk: Strangers sleeping in your home. Regulation. And hotels with actual marketing budgets.

outcome.headline: The weird one wins
outcome.summary: Airbnb turned a spare-room hack into a global category. The early idea sounded embarrassing; the trust layer made it inevitable.
outcome.lesson: The best ideas often sound embarrassing at seed stage. Distribution and trust were the real product.

milestones: Airbnb launches. Critics call it a couch-surfing gimmick.
One million nights booked. The flywheel starts to spin.
International expansion. Hotels start paying attention.
Regulators circle. The model adapts city by city.
A travel giant is born — and the weirdness becomes the brand.

slack.tagline: A failed video game that accidentally became work software.
slack.description: Tiny Speck was building a multiplayer game called Glitch. The game died; the internal chat tool built to survive it did not. Slack launched to the public in 2013.
slack.pitch: Team chat that people actually enjoy. Channels, search, integrations — one place for work to happen.
slack.risk: A crowded workplace software market, giant incumbents, and a team that just shut down a game.

outcome.headline: The pivot that printed
outcome.summary: Slack grew to millions of daily users and was acquired by Salesforce for $27.7B in 2021. The chat tool outlived the game that birthed it.
outcome.lesson: A pivot is not a failure. It is a second shot with better information.

milestones: Slack opens to the public. Teams invite other teams.
One million daily active users. The bottom-up flywheel hums.
Enterprise deals begin. The fun chat app grows up.
Slack becomes a verb in offices everywhere.
Salesforce comes knocking with $27.7B.

twitter.tagline: A side project inside a failed podcast company.
twitter.description: Odeo was a podcast platform that got steamrolled by Apple. During a hack week, Jack Dorsey pitched a tiny status-update tool. The first tweet: 'just setting up my twttr.'
twitter.pitch: Send a short update to your friends. 140 characters. No friction, no blog, no pressure.
twitter.risk: No revenue model, a niche of early adopters, and a name that sounds like a bird noise.

outcome.headline: 140 characters, global reach
outcome.summary: Twitter became the world's real-time public square, went public in 2013 at a $14B+ valuation, and reshaped media, politics, and memes.
outcome.lesson: Simple products can hide enormous network effects. The early dip was noise, not the story.

milestones: SXSW explodes. A 140-character update feels like the future.
The fail whale era. Growth is real, uptime is not.
Hashtags and retweets turn users into a distribution engine.
News breaks on Twitter first. The public square forms.
IPO. The side project is worth billions.

deck.title: Swipe with
deck.body: Right means you would take a meeting. Left means pass. Judge the pitch, not the polish — founders only get a few seconds.
deck.investAria: I would invest in this startup
deck.hint: Drag the card, tap a button, or use
deck.ownTitle: Your pitch is on the board.
deck.ownBody: Founders cannot swipe on their own startup. Share the board with the room and watch the votes come in.
deck.reviewedBody: Meetings: {invested}. Passes: {passed}. Your votes are now part of the room's signal.
deck.resetConfirm: Clear all your votes and review the deck again?

submit.title: Put your idea
submit.body: One card, five fields, zero pitch-deck software. It goes live on the board immediately.
submit.pitchPlaceholder: What do you do, who is it for, and why now? Make us feel the problem in one breath.
submit.privacy: Your name and pitch are visible to event participants. You cannot vote on your own card.
submit.previewPitch: Your 30-second pitch will appear here. Make the problem feel real, then show the wedge.
tips: A problem we can picture in five seconds.
A wedge that makes sense with your funding ask.
Proof of life: a pilot, a waitlist, a first customer.
submit.successLive: It is now part of the deck. Other participants can swipe on it — and you cannot vote for yourself.
submit.successOffline: The live board is offline, so your card is saved on this device for now. It will still appear in your local results.
submit.errorSummary: A few fields need attention before this goes live.

errors.titleShort: Give your startup a name (3+ characters).
errors.pitchShort: Tell us a little more — at least 30 characters.
errors.niche: Pick a niche from the list.
errors.marketShort: Describe who this is for (3+ characters).

errors.founder: Add a founder or team name.

results.title: What investors
results.body: Every swipe becomes a signal. See which pitches cut through, which niches carry the room, and how the size of the ask changes the answer.

results.newOnBoard: New on the board — waiting for its first swipe.
results.resetConfirm: Clear all your votes and start the deck again?
results.missingBody: Swipe a few pitches and we will show you whether you are a conviction investor, a selective skeptic, or a very tough room.
results.nicheHeatBody: Which categories make the room lean in.

results.bucketBestLarge: {range} pitches convert at {rate}% — ambition is not being penalised in this room.
results.bucketBestSmall: {range} pitches convert at {rate}% — lower risk is clearly attractive.
results.bucketBestMid: {range} pitches convert at {rate}% — there is a sweet spot in the middle.

conviction.label: Conviction Investor
conviction.blurb: You say yes more than most. That gives founders momentum, but it also means you need a strong filter for the ideas you do not back.

balanced.label: Balanced Backer
balanced.blurb: You are open, not automatic. Roughly half the room earns your interest — a useful mix of curiosity and discernment.

skeptic.label: Selective Skeptic
skeptic.blurb: You make founders work for it. Fewer yes votes, but the ones you give carry more signal.

tough.label: Tough Room
tough.blurb: You passed on almost everything. Either the bar is high, or the pitches have work to do. Both are useful data.

attention.title: Attention is not evenly distributed
attention.body: {startup} converts {rate}% of views into interest — {invests} yes votes from {total} swipes. In a deck of six, being memorable matters as much as being good.

nicheMoment.title: {niche} is having a moment
nicheMoment.body: Pitches in {niche} earn a {rate}% invest rate across {total} votes. The room is rewarding the category as much as the company — a real advantage, and a real trend risk.

smallYes.title: Smaller cheques are easier to say yes to
smallYes.body: Startups asking under $20k get a {smallRate}% invest rate versus {largeRate}% for asks above $35k. Lower risk is attractive — but the biggest companies rarely start cheap.

bigYes.title: Big asks are not scaring the room
bigYes.body: Startups asking above $35k still convert at {largeRate}%, ahead of the small-ask group at {smallRate}%. Ambition is not being penalised here.

campus-bite.title: CampusBite
campus-bite.pitch: Half-price meals from campus cafés, rescued before closing time. Students save money, kitchens earn from food that would be binned, and nobody has to eat another sad meal deal.

notewave.title: NoteWave
notewave.pitch: AI that turns messy lecture recordings into structured notes, flashcards, and a weekly revision plan — trained on your course, in your university's own language.

greenloop.title: GreenLoop
greenloop.pitch: Reusable takeaway boxes with a €2 deposit, tracked in an app. Cafés ditch single-use packaging without hiring extra staff, and students get their deposit back.

skillswap.title: SkillSwap
skillswap.pitch: A skill-bartering board where students trade an hour of guitar for an hour of calculus. No money, just verified campus reputation and a reason to meet people offline.
skillswap.targetMarket: Students in their first two years

mindfulu.title: MindfulU
mindfulu.pitch: Five-minute, exam-week mental health check-ins with peer-trained responders and instant links to campus support. Private by design, built for the 2am panic before a deadline.

rentmate.title: RentMate
rentmate.pitch: Verified student housing matching, rent splitting, and contract checks in one place. No more Facebook groups, ghost landlords, or discovering the kitchen is a curtain.
